questions.question_text: Which of the following is NOT typically associated with school refusal?
questions.explanation:
School refusal is characterised by refusal to go to school or stay in school, even when under pressure from parents and school authorities. It is not a psychiatric disorder per se and can have many causes; it is considered a problem rather than a diagnosis. School refusal is generally associated with separation anxiety and may co-occur with anxiety and depressive disorders. It is usually not an isolated problem. These children typically avoid many other social situations, and often display tantrums, desperate pleas, and somatic complaints (e.g. headaches, stomach aches, nausea). School refusal may occur in a young child who is first entering school or in an older child or adolescent who is making a transition into a new grade or school.
Ref: Boland R, Verduin M. Kaplan and Sadock's Synopsis of Psychiatry, 12th Edition. 2022. p. 896.
Elliott JG, Place M. Practitioner review: school refusal: developments in conceptualisation and treatment since 2000. Journal of Child Psychology and Psychiatry. 2019 Jan;60(1):4-15.
The correct answer is: Educational underachievement

questions.question_text: Which of the following childhood psychiatric conditions has the highest heritability factor?
questions.explanation:
ADHD has the highest heritability among the listed conditions. ADHD has a heritability of 70-80%, and the risk of ADHD in siblings is 2-3x increased. Rates are increased in premature babies (especially extreme prematurity), babies born to mothers who used substances during pregnancy (e.g. tobacco or alcohol), following head injury, and in some genetic and metabolic disorders. None of the proposed prenatal risk factors have been confirmed as causal for ADHD.
Ref: Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press; 2019 Jul 30. p. 668.
Sciberras E, Mulraney M, Silva D, Coghill D. Prenatal risk factors and the etiology of ADHD—review of existing evidence. Current psychiatry reports. 2017 Jan 1;19(1):1.
The correct answer is: ADHD

questions.question_text: When compared to younger children, which one of the following features of depression is seen more commonly in older children and adolescents?
questions.explanation:
Younger children (ages 3-8) with depression may have trouble verbalising feelings but show marked decreased interest in play, increased somatic complaints, and crying or shouting outbursts. Older children and adolescents (ages 9-18) with depression may have low self-esteem, guilt, hopelessness, increased boredom, feelings of wanting to run away, and decreased grades and poor school performance.
Ref: Mullen S. Major depressive disorder in children and adolescents. Mental Health Clinician. 2018 Nov;8(6):275-83.
The correct answer is: Low self-esteem

questions.question_text: In children with PANDAS, which of the following is least common?
questions.explanation:
Paediatric autoimmune neuropsychiatric disorder associated with streptococcal infections (PANDAS) is characterised by the sudden and dramatic onset of obsessive-compulsive disorder, tic symptoms, or severely restricted food intake and neuropsychiatric comorbidity, also of sudden and severe onset, following group A streptococci (GAS) infection. Common comorbidities include anxiety (including separation anxiety); emotional lability and/or depression; irritability, aggression and/or severely oppositional behaviours; behavioural (developmental) regression; deterioration in school performance (ADHD-like symptoms, memory deficits, cognitive changes); sensory or motor abnormalities; somatic signs and symptoms (including sleep disturbances, enuresis, or increased urinary frequency). Nearly ⅓ of children endorse concerns related to suicide. The term Pediatric Acute-onset Neuropsychiatric Syndrome (PANS) is used when the etiology or mechanism of the abrupt onset is unknown.
Ref: Warrilow A, Morton M. Autoimmune disorders in child psychiatry: keeping up with the field. BJPsych Advances. 2015 Nov;21(6):367-76.
Cabrera-Mendoza B et al. Diagnosis in PANDAS: An Update. Current Psychiatry Research and Reviews Formerly: Current Psychiatry Reviews. 2019 Dec 1;15(4):237-47.
The correct answer is: Psychosis

questions.question_text: All of the following statements about the Wechsler Intelligence Scale for Children are true except

options.text: Object assembly and coding are two subtests used to assess performance IQ
It can be given to children from 6 to 17 years of age
It is helpful for the assessment of general intelligence in school-age children
Tests are divided into 'verbal' and 'performance' categories, yielding a verbal and performance IQ
Twelve primary subtests are usually used, measuring different aspects of the child's ability

correct_answer.text: Twelve primary subtests are usually used, measuring different aspects of the child's ability

correct_answers.text: Twelve primary subtests are usually used, measuring different aspects of the child's ability

questions.explanation:
Wechsler Intelligence Scale for Children (third edition):
-       Most widely used test of intelligence for school-age children and adolescents
-       Can be given to children from 6 to 17 years of age
-       Yields a verbal IQ, performance IQ, and combined full-scale IQ
-       Verbal subtests (5): vocabulary, information, arithmetic, similarities, comprehension (and one supplemental: digit span)
-       Performance subtests (5): block design, picture completion, picture arrangement, object assembly, coding (and two supplemental: mazes and symbol search)
-       The IQ computation does not include the scores of the supplemental subtests
Ref: Boland R, Verduin M. Kaplan and Sadock's Synopsis of Psychiatry, 12th Edition. 2022. p. 81.
The correct answer is: Twelve primary subtests are usually used, measuring different aspects of the child's ability

questions.question_text: About 99% of children are dry by day (no daytime wetting) by the age of
questions.explanation:
By the age of 5 years, only 1% of children have problems with daytime wetting. However, nocturnal enuresis can still affect 15-22% boys and 7-15% girls at the age of 7 years. There is a reduction in rates of enuresis with time, but a small minority continues to have problems into adulthood.
Ref: Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press; 2019 Jul 30. p. 680.
The correct answer is: 5 years

questions.question_text: Which of the following is considered the treatment of choice for children with school refusal?
questions.explanation:
Cognitive behavioural therapy (CBT) continues to be the therapy of choice for school refusal (with a shift in emphasis over time from standardised to individualised approaches, and the incorporation of exposure techniques). CBT has largely replaced psychoanalytic approaches as the preferred method of treatment for school refusal. While it seems that family work is an essential aspect of treatment for school refusal, controlled studies examining family-based therapies have been rare and findings have been equivocal. Instead, family work is now seen as more appropriately embedded within a CBT programme. There is little evidence to support the use of medication as part of a treatment programme for school refusal.
Of note, a continuing divide exists between those who argue for and against a conceptual merger in which the term 'school refusal' or 'school refusal behaviour' includes both those anxious about attending school, and those who would historically be classed as 'truants'. Some commentators have queried whether those labelled as truants are treated less sympathetically than those whose nonattendance is considered to be the consequence of high levels of anxiety. The impact of labelling can result in differential access to professional services, and forms of intervention, with truancy often more likely to result in legal proceedings that may reflect a punitive, rather than a therapeutic, focus.
Ref: Elliott JG, Place M. Practitioner review: school refusal: developments in conceptualisation and treatment since 2000. Journal of Child Psychology and Psychiatry. 2019 Jan;60(1):4-15.
The correct answer is: Cognitive behavioural therapy

questions.question_text: Which of the following is true about Tourette syndrome?

options.text: Mean age of onset is 12 years
Females are more affected than males
Diagnosed by having both motor and vocal tics for 6 months
Diagnosed by having both motor and vocal tics for 12 months
Antipsychotics are the first line treatment

correct_answer.text: Diagnosed by having both motor and vocal tics for 12 months

correct_answers.text: Diagnosed by having both motor and vocal tics for 12 months

questions.explanation:
Tourette syndrome is a complex neuropsychiatric disorder with childhood onset characterised by multiple motor and one or more vocal tics, present for at least a year. Males are more commonly affected (3-4:1, male:female). The age of onset is 2-21 years, with a mean age of 7 years. All patients should receive psychoeducation, reassurance, and explanation. In mild cases and young people this may suffice. Behavioural methods (that may be useful alone or in combination with medications) include habit reversal training, comprehensive behavioural intervention for tics, exposure and response prevention, and self-hypnosis. Medication is warranted if tics cause distress or are functionally disabling and is also used in the treatment of many of the co-morbidities.
Ref: Robertson MM. Tourette syndrome in children and adolescents: aetiology, presentation and treatment. BJPsych Advances. 2016 May;22(3):165-75.
Taylor DM, Barnes TRE, Young AH. The Maudsley Prescribing Guidelines in Psychiatry, 14th Edition. 2021. p. 587.
The correct answer is: Diagnosed by having both motor and vocal tics for 12 months

questions.question_text: Blockade of which of the following receptors can reduce vocal and motor tics seen in Tourette syndrome?
questions.explanation:
Evidence suggests that dopamine super-sensitivity, specifically involving nigrostriatal dopamine D2 receptors, leads to tics. Agents that reduce dopamine activity suppress tics, while dopamine-enhancing substances (like cocaine) exacerbate them.
Ref: Kaufman DM, Geyer HL, Milstein MJ, Rosengard JL. Kaufman's Clinical Neurology for Psychiatrists, 9th Edition. 2023. p. 444.
Nomura Y. Pharmacological therapy for Tourette syndrome: What medicine can do and cannot do. Biomedical Journal. 2021 Sep 20.
The correct answer is: D2 receptors

questions.question_text: Which of the following is thought to have the least genetic loading/heritability?
questions.explanation:
Of those listed, conduct disorder is thought to have the least genetic loading. Still, there is now solid evidence from twin and adoption studies that conduct problems assessed both dimensionally and categorically are substantially heritable.
Ref: National Institute for Health and Clinical Excellence. The NICE guideline on the recognition, intervention and management of antisocial behaviour and conduct disorders in children and young people. Updated 2017.
The correct answer is: Conduct disorder

questions.question_text: Which one of the following is a true statement about bipolar disorder in children and adolescents?

options.text: 60-70% of initial presentations are a manic episode
Manic children typically present with atypical or mixed features
Lamotrigine is used if treatment resistant manic episodes are present
The course is often episodic and of brief duration

correct_answer.text: Manic children typically present with atypical or mixed features

correct_answers.text: Manic children typically present with atypical or mixed features

questions.explanation:
Children experiencing a manic episode typically present with atypical or mixed features characterised by irritability, labile mood, and behavioural problems. Periods of depression are common, and early-onset bipolar disorder more often presents with depression than in adult-onset bipolar. Early-onset bipolar may be characterised by non-episodic, chronic, ultra-rapid cycling, mixed irritable and manic states. The prevalence in adolescents is approximately 1% and as high as 6% when including soft subsyndromal symptoms. M>F in childhood cases; M=F in adolescents. For the treatment of mania and hypomania in youth, NICE guidelines suggest following the same recommendations as adults: second-generation antipsychotics (SGAs) may be used as first-line treatment, and mood stabilisers can be added after failure of two trials of SGAs. Lamotrigine has not been studied in RCTs for the treatment of acute bipolar depression in children and adolescents and is not recommended as first-line. It is not recommended in the treatment of manic episodes.
Ref: Findling RL et al. Progress in diagnosis and treatment of bipolar disorder among children and adolescents: an international perspective. Evidence-based mental health. 2018 Nov 1;21(4):177-81.
National Institute for Health and Clinical Excellence. The NICE guideline on the assessment and management of bipolar disorder in adults, children and young people in primary and secondary care. Updated edition 2020.
Taylor DM, Barnes TRE, Young AH. The Maudsley Prescribing Guidelines in Psychiatry, 14th Edition. 2021. pp. 547-551.
The correct answer is: Manic children typically present with atypical or mixed features

questions.question_text: Which of the following risk factors is associated with autism spectrum disorder?
questions.explanation:
The prevalence of autism spectrum disorder in preterm infants is considerably higher than the general population.
Ref: Agrawal S, Rao SC, Bulsara MK, Patole SK. Prevalence of autism spectrum disorder in preterm infants: a meta-analysis. Pediatrics. 2018 Sep 1;142(3):e20180134.
The correct answer is: Premature birth

questions.question_text: Which of the following treatments is most recommended for treating PTSD in children?
questions.explanation:
Within one month of a traumatic event, consider active monitoring or individual trauma-focused CBT for children and adolescents. >1 month after a traumatic event, the treatment of choice for PTSD is individual trauma-focused CBT. Consider EMDR for those ages 7-17 who present >3 months after a traumatic event only if they do not respond to or engage with trauma-focused CBT. Do NOT use psychologically-focused debriefing for the prevention or treatment of PTSD in children and adolescents. Do NOT offer drug treatments for the prevention or treatment of PTSD in children and young people under 18 years.
Ref: National Institute for Health and Clinical Excellence. NICE guideline Post-traumatic stress disorder 2018.
The correct answer is: Trauma-focused CBT

questions.question_text: The prevalence of ADHD in the UK is
questions.explanation:
The UK prevalence for ADHD is just under 5%; 3-4% in boys and just under 1% in girls (four times more common in boys).
Ref: Hill P. Attention-deficit hyperactivity disorder in children and adolescents: Assessment and treatment. BJPsych Advances. 2015 Jan;21(1):23-30.
The correct answer is: 2-5%

questions.question_text: The sex distribution is equal in which of the following conditions?
questions.explanation:
School refusal is characterised by refusal to go to school or stay in school, even when under pressure from parents and school authorities. It is not a psychiatric disorder per se and can have many causes; it is considered a problem rather than a diagnosis. The incidence in children and adolescents reported to be 1-5%, with the sex distribution equal.
Ref: Boland R, Verduin M. Kaplan and Sadock's Synopsis of Psychiatry, 12th Edition. 2022. p. 896.
Elliott JG, Place M. Practitioner review: school refusal: developments in conceptualisation and treatment since 2000. Journal of Child Psychology and Psychiatry. 2019 Jan;60(1):4-15.
The correct answer is: School refusal

questions.question_text: In a 7-year-old child with uncomplicated Tourette syndrome, the drug treatment of choice is
questions.explanation:
Tourette syndrome is a complex neuropsychiatric disorder with childhood onset characterised by multiple motor and one or more vocal tics, present for at least a year. All patients should receive psychoeducation, reassurance, and explanation. In mild cases and young people this may suffice. Behavioural methods (that may be useful alone or in combination with medications) include habit reversal training, comprehensive behavioural intervention for tics, exposure and response prevention, and self-hypnosis. Medication is warranted if tics cause distress or are functionally disabling and is also used in the treatment of many of the co-morbidities. Adverse effects of antipsychotics may outweigh beneficial effects in the treatment of tics and so it is recommended that clonidine or guanfacine are always tried first. Antipsychotics may, however, be more effective than adrenergic alpha-2 agonists in alleviating tics in some individuals.
Ref: Robertson MM. Tourette syndrome in children and adolescents: aetiology, presentation and treatment. BJPsych Advances. 2016 May;22(3):165-75.
Taylor DM, Barnes TRE, Young AH. The Maudsley Prescribing Guidelines in Psychiatry, 14th Edition. 2021. pp. 587-588.
The correct answer is: Clonidine

questions.question_text: What percentage of patients with autism have intellectual disability?
questions.explanation:
80% of patients with autism have mild to moderate intellectual disability. In general terms, 1-2% of those with autism have a 'normal' life; 5-20% have a 'borderline' prognosis (i.e. varying degrees independence), but 70% are totally dependent upon support.
Ref: Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press; 2019 Jul 30. p. 822.
The correct answer is: 70-80%

questions.question_text: The ratio of prevalence of ADHD in males to females is
questions.explanation:
The UK prevalence for ADHD is just under 5%; 3-4% in boys and just under 1% in girls (four times more common in boys).
Ref: Hill P. Attention-deficit hyperactivity disorder in children and adolescents: Assessment and treatment. BJPsych Advances. 2015 Jan;21(1):23-30.
The correct answer is: 4 to 1

questions.question_text: Which of the following is not a characteristic feature of PTSD in children?

options.text: Intrusive re-experiencing of a traumatic event

questions.explanation:
The clinical presentation of PTSD in children may include the following:
Compulsive repetitive play representing part of the trauma and failing to relieve anxiety
Recurrent, involuntary, and intrusive distressing memories of the traumatic event(s)
Intrusive re-experiencing of the event(s)
Dissociative reactions (e.g. flashbacks) in which the child feels or acts as if the traumatic event(s) were recurring
Avoidance
Nightmares, sleep terrors, and/or difficulty going to sleep
Constriction of play
Social withdrawal
Restricted affect
Loss of acquired developmental skills, especially language regression and toilet training
Hyperarousal, hypervigilance, exaggerated startle response
Decreased concentration and attention
New separation anxiety
New aggression
Ref: Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press; 2019 Jul 30. p. 688.
American Psychiatric Association. Diagnostic and statistical manual of mental disorders (DSM-5®). American Psychiatric Pub; 2013 May 22.
The correct answer is: Selective amnesia for the event

questions.question_text: A child is hyperactive and distractible in school and at home. Choose the risk factor associated with the development of this condition.
questions.explanation:
ADHD has a heritability of 70-80%, and the risk of ADHD in siblings is 2-3x increased. Rates are increased in premature babies (especially extreme prematurity), babies born to mothers who used substances during pregnancy (e.g. tobacco or alcohol), following head injury, and in some genetic and metabolic disorders. None of the proposed prenatal risk factors have been confirmed as causal for ADHD.
Ref: Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press; 2019 Jul 30. p. 668.
Sciberras E, Mulraney M, Silva D, Coghill D. Prenatal risk factors and the etiology of ADHD—review of existing evidence. Current psychiatry reports. 2017 Jan 1;19(1):1.
The correct answer is: Maternal smoking in pregnancy

questions.question_text: A 14-year-old boy was interviewed to identify the presence of psychiatric disease. What scale could be used again at the age of 20?
questions.explanation:
The Clinical Interview Schedule-Revised (CIS-R) asks questions about a range of symptoms and can be used to assign ICD diagnoses of psychiatric disorders.
Ref: Cornish RP, John A, Boyd A, Tilling K, Macleod J. Defining adolescent common mental disorders using electronic primary care data: a comparison with outcomes measured using the CIS-R. BMJ open. 2016 Dec 1;6(12).
The correct answer is: Clinical Interview Schedule-Revised

questions.question_text: You want to follow the progress in symptoms for a period of 3 years in patients diagnosed with depression at the age of 14. Which clinical instrument is most useful?

options.text: Child and Adolescent Functional Assessment Scale

correct_answer.text: Child and Adolescent Functional Assessment Scale

correct_answers.text: Child and Adolescent Functional Assessment Scale

questions.explanation:
The Child and Adolescent Functional Assessment Scale (CAFAS) is a clinician-rated measure of functional impairment in youth 6-17 years of age, secondary to behavioural, emotional, or substance use problems.
Ref: Boydell KM, Barwick M, Ferguson HB, Haines R. A feasibility study to assess service providers' perspectives regarding the use of the Child and Adolescent Functional Assessment Scale in Ontario. The Journal of Behavioral Health Services & Research. 2005 Jan 1;32(1):105-9.
The correct answer is: Child and Adolescent Functional Assessment Scale

questions.question_text: Which of the following blood abnormalities is commonly seen in anorexia nervosa?
questions.explanation:
Anaemia, leukopenia, and although less frequently, thrombocytopaenia are possible haematological complications of anorexia nervosa (AN) considered strictly secondary to chronic malnutrition. Usually, anaemia in AN is normocytic and normochromic, and leukopenia is characterised by lymphocytopenia or neutropenia; thrombocytopaenia may also be present.
Ref: De Filippo E et al. Hematological complications in anorexia nervosa. European Journal of Clinical Nutrition. 2016 Nov;70(11):1305-8.
The correct answer is: Normocytic normochromic anaemia

questions.question_text: What is the average age of onset of schizophrenia?
questions.explanation:
The average age of onset of schizophrenia is 23 years of age in men and 26 years of age in women.
Ref: Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press; 2019 Jul 30. p. 190.
The correct answer is: 25

questions.question_text: Which one of the following statements about suicide and adolescents is true?

options.text: 1% of adolescents who attempt suicide repeat within a year.
Hanging is the most common method of suicide in UK adolescents.
Suicide is the leading cause of death amongst adolescents.
Female suicides are more than male suicides in UK adolescents.
Most first attempts at suicide by adolescents are pre-planned.

correct_answer.text: Hanging is the most common method of suicide in UK adolescents.

correct_answers.text: Hanging is the most common method of suicide in UK adolescents.

questions.explanation:
Rates of suicide in the UK have increased among adolescents by approximately 7.9% each year between 2010 and 2017. Rates among females have increased at a higher rate, though absolute number of deaths is still lower among young women than young men. Suicide is the third leading cause of death for adolescents, following accidents and homicides. Hanging is the most common method of suicide in the UK for both children and adolescents. Half of suicide attempts are first attempts and most are impulsive, with only 25% having evidence of planning (impulsivity is linked to sensation-seeking and increased risk-taking behaviour in adolescence). 10% of adolescents who attempt suicide repeat within a year.
Ref: Correia R, Jackson D. Risk to self: identifying and managing risk of suicide and self-harm. BJPsych Advances. 2020:1-11.
Bould H et al. Rising suicide rates among adolescents in England and Wales. The Lancet. 2019 Jul 13;394(10193):116-7.
Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press; 2019 Jul 30. pp. 698-699.
The correct answer is: Hanging is the most common method of suicide in UK adolescents.

questions.question_text: The prevalence of suicidal ideation in the past year for the adolescent cohort in Britain is
questions.explanation:
Suicidal ideation (without deliberate self-harm) in the past year was reported by 15.0% of an adolescent cohort in UK (school pupils - self-report). This was more common in females (22%) than males (8.5%) (Odds ratio 3.1. Hawton et al., 2002).
Global statistics are also comparable with the aggregate lifetime prevalence and 12-month prevalence being 6% and 4.5% for attempts, 9.9% and 7.5% for plans and 18% and 14.2% respectively for ideations. Non-suicidal self-injury has higher lifetime and 12-month prevalence among children and adolescents globally = 22.1% and 19.5% respectively.
Ref: Lim, K.S., et al., 2019. Global lifetime and 12-month prevalence of suicidal behavior, deliberate self-harm and non-suicidal self-injury in children and adolescents between 1989 and 2018: a meta-analysis. International journal of environmental research and public health, 16(22), p.4581.
Hawton K, Rodham K, Evans E, Weatherall R. Deliberate self harm in adolescents: self report survey in schools in England. Bmj. 2002 Nov 23;325(7374):1207-11.
The correct answer is: 15%

questions.question_text: The most common psychiatric emergency seen in the child and adolescent population is
questions.explanation:
Numerous reasons are given for emergency presentations, but most commonly the goal is the assessment of self-injurious thoughts and behaviours (SITB). In addition to non-suicidal self-injury (NSSI), which is carried out without the intention to die, suicidal behaviour, in which the person has at least to some degree the intention to die, is defined as SITB. Since the intention to die is often ambivalent in patients, there is overlap between NSSI and suicidal behaviour.
Ref: Kandsperger S et al. Suicidality presented to a child and adolescent psychiatry emergency service: increasing rate and changing characteristics. Frontiers in psychiatry. 2021:1195.
The correct answer is: Suicidal behaviour

questions.question_text: Preschoolers and school-age children who stutter exhibit an increased incidence of which of the following conditions?
questions.explanation:
Very young children who stutter typically show some delay in the development of language and articulation without additional disorders of speech and language. Preschoolers and school-age children who stutter exhibit an increased incidence of social anxiety, school refusal, and other anxiety symptoms. Older children who stutter also do not necessarily have co-morbid speech and language disorders, but often manifest anxiety symptoms and disorders. When stuttering persists into adolescence, social isolation occurs at higher rates than in the general adolescent population.
Ref: Boland R, Verduin M. Kaplan and Sadock's Synopsis of Psychiatry, 12th Edition. 2022. p. 118.
The correct answer is: Social anxiety

questions.question_text: The overall prevalence of psychiatric problems in adolescence is
questions.explanation:
Adolescence, defined as a transitional phase between ages 10 and 19, is sometimes perceived as a phase of life with no health problems. However, approximately 20% of adolescents experience a mental health problem, most commonly depression or anxiety.
Ref: Silva SA et al. Common mental disorders prevalence in adolescents: A systematic review and meta-analyses. PloS one. 2020 Apr 23;15(4):e0232007.
The correct answer is: 16-20%

questions.question_text: With appropriate consultation and monitoring, which of the following medications can be prescribed for children with ADHD and congenital heart disease?
questions.explanation:
Children with congenital heart disease (CHD) have been shown to be at increased risk for ADHD. Case reports have led to concern regarding the use of ADHD medications in children with underlying CHD. However, multiple large studies have demonstrated no increased risk of sudden cardiac death in children on stimulant medications or atomoxetine. Typical cardiovascular changes are a mild increase in heart rate and/or blood pressure that are rarely haemodynamically significant. Prior to prescribing, an ECG and cardiology opinion should be sought if the patient has a history of CHD.
Ref: Pierick AR et al. Treatment of attention deficit/hyperactivity disorder in children with CHD. Cardiology in the Young. 2021 Jun;31(6):969-72.
Taylor DM, Barnes TRE, Young AH. The Maudsley Prescribing Guidelines in Psychiatry, 14th Edition. 2021. p. 570.
The correct answer is: All of the listed options

questions.question_text: Which autoimmune disorder is associated with OCD in children?
questions.explanation:
Paediatric autoimmune neuropsychiatric disorder associated with streptococcal infections (PANDAS) is characterised by the sudden and dramatic onset of obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD), tic symptoms, or severely restricted food intake and neuropsychiatric comorbidity, also of sudden and severe onset, following group A beta-haemolytic streptococcal (GABHS) infection. The pathophysiological hypothesis in PANDAS states that GABHS infections trigger the production of antibodies that, in turn, cross-react against the central nervous system and cause tics and OCD symptoms. In contrast to Tourette syndrome, where a preceding infection may exacerbate symptoms, in PANDAS the streptococcal infection and its induced cross-reacting antibodies are proposed as the cause of the symptoms. The term Pediatric Acute-onset Neuropsychiatric Syndrome (PANS) is used when the aetiology or mechanism of the abrupt onset is unknown.
Ref: Warrilow A, Morton M. Autoimmune disorders in child psychiatry: keeping up with the field. BJPsych Advances. 2015 Nov;21(6):367-76.
Cabrera-Mendoza B et al. Diagnosis in PANDAS: An Update. Current Psychiatry Research and Reviews Formerly: Current Psychiatry Reviews. 2019 Dec 1;15(4):237-47.
Gilbert DL et al. A pediatric neurology perspective on pediatric autoimmune neuropsychiatric disorder associated with streptococcal infection and pediatric acute-onset neuropsychiatric syndrome. The Journal of pediatrics. 2018 Aug 1;199:243-51.
The correct answer is: PANDAS

questions.question_text: In the aetiology of disruptive behaviour disorders (DBDs; including oppositional defiant disorder and conduct disorder), which of the following statements regarding parenting styles is true?

options.text: Parenting styles are not key factors in shaping DBDs in children
Harsh parenting is not associated with DBDs in children and adolescents
When siblings live together in the same family, they experience the same parenting
If one child in a family has DBD, their sibling(s) will also have DBD
The presence of DBD in a family is a risk factor for externalising problems in siblings

correct_answer.text: The presence of DBD in a family is a risk factor for externalising problems in siblings

correct_answers.text: The presence of DBD in a family is a risk factor for externalising problems in siblings

questions.explanation:
Studies have indicated that parenting styles are key factors in shaping disruptive behaviour disorders (DBDs; including oppositional defiant disorder and conduct disorder) in children. Specifically, the use of harsh parenting, which includes coercive, controlling, and punitive methods, the use of verbal and physical aggression, combined with low warmth and poor positive parenting, are associated with DBDs as well as more general externalising disorders in children and adolescents. Even when siblings live in the same family context, they can experience different relationships with the same parents, and be exposed to different levels of harsh and supporting parenting, thus resulting in different adjustments. The clinical manifestation of DBDs (which includes irritability, aggression, and temper outbursts) is a risk factor for the development of externalising problems in siblings.
Ref: Smorti M et al. Parenting and sibling relationships in family with disruptive behavior disorders. Are non-clinical siblings more vulnerable for emotional and behavioral problems?. Brain Sciences. 2021 Oct 1;11(10):1308.
The correct answer is: The presence of DBD in a family is a risk factor for externalising problems in siblings

questions.question_text: In operant conditioning with children, shaping refers to

options.text: Reinforcing positive behaviour; ignoring negative behaviour
Punishing negative behaviour; praising positive behaviour
Neither reinforcing nor punishing observed behaviours
Gradual reinforcement of behaviours approximating the desired outcome
Differential reinforcement of behaviours other than the desired outcome

correct_answer.text: Gradual reinforcement of behaviours approximating the desired outcome

correct_answers.text: Gradual reinforcement of behaviours approximating the desired outcome

questions.explanation:
Shaping is used to produce a complex behaviour that is not in the child's initial repertoire. Initially, component parts of the desired behaviour are rewarded, then reward is limited to behaviour that approximates the desired outcome. As appropriate behaviour appears, it is rewarded only if it is 'in the right direction', and further reward is contingent upon continued advancement until the child is only rewarded once the entire behaviour is performed.
Ref: Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press; 2019 Jul 30. p. 907.
The correct answer is: Gradual reinforcement of behaviours approximating the desired outcome

questions.question_text: Which of the following drugs has the best evidence for use in childhood depression?
questions.explanation:
UK guidelines (particularly NICE, updated 2019) recommend a stepped-care approach in the treatment of childhood depression. 5–11-year-old children should only be offered fluoxetine when psychological therapy has been ineffective. Second-line medications are sertraline and citalopram. Paroxetine and venlafaxine should not be used, as they have the strongest association with suicide risk (especially with adolescents). TCAs should not be used; they are not useful in young children and there is only low-quality marginal evidence to support their use in adolescents.
Ref: National Institute for Health and Clinical Excellence. The NICE guideline on the identification and management of depression in children and young people. 2019.
The correct answer is: Fluoxetine

questions.question_text: Most children with selective mutism also meet diagnostic criteria for which of the following disorders?
questions.explanation:
Selective mutism is characterised by the persistent failure to speak in specific settings (e.g. school) where there is an expectation to speak. It begins after normal speech has been acquired, and there is full use of language at home/with family. Patients may remain wholly silent or near-silent, in some cases only whispering in a school setting. In rare cases, a child is mute at home but not in school. Social anxiety is almost always present.
Ref: Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press; 2019 Jul 30. p. 687.
Boland R, Verduin M. Kaplan and Sadock's Synopsis of Psychiatry, 12th Edition. 2022. p. 201.
The correct answer is: Social anxiety disorder

questions.question_text: Which one of the following statements about Rett syndrome is true?

options.text: Characterised by progressive loss of acquired abilities
Apparent lack of normal development in the first 2 years of life

correct_answer.text: Characterised by progressive loss of acquired abilities

correct_answers.text: Characterised by progressive loss of acquired abilities

questions.explanation:
Rett Syndrome:
·   Believed to be caused by dominant X-linked gene
·   Degenerative disorder that almost exclusively affects females
·   Initially normal development
·   Ages 1-4 yrs: purposeful hand movements & spoken language lost; stereotypical hand movements (hand-wringing) & autism
·   Ataxia, facial grimacing, teeth-grinding, and loss of speech
·   Irregular respiration with episodes of hyperventilation, apnea, and breath-holding
·   Progressive gait disturbance, scoliosis, and seizures
·   Sleep disturbances are common; initial and/or intermediate insomnia, leading to excessive daytime sleep
Ref: Boland R, Verduin M. Kaplan and Sadock's Synopsis of Psychiatry, 12th Edition. 2022. p. 103.
Persico AM et al. The psychopharmacology of autism spectrum disorder and Rett syndrome. In Handbook of clinical neurology 2019 Jan 1 (Vol. 165, pp. 391-414). Elsevier.
The correct answer is: Characterised by progressive loss of acquired abilities

questions.question_text: Which of the following disorders is characterised by impaired ability to recognise words, slow and inaccurate reading, and poor comprehension?

options.text: Developmental language disorder with impairment of mainly pragmatic language
Developmental language disorder with impairment of receptive and expressive language
Developmental language disorder with impairment of mainly expressive language
Developmental learning disorder with impairment in reading
Developmental learning disorder with impairment in written expression

correct_answer.text: Developmental learning disorder with impairment in reading

correct_answers.text: Developmental learning disorder with impairment in reading

questions.explanation:
Developmental learning disorder with impairment in reading is characterised by significant and persistent difficulties in learning academic skills related to reading, such as word reading accuracy, reading fluency, and reading comprehension. The individual's performance in reading is markedly below what would be expected for chronological age and level of intellectual functioning and results in significant impairment in functioning. 4% of school-age children are affected. There is male predominance [4:1] and often a family history. Approximately 20% of children have co-morbid CD or ADHD.
Ref: International Statistical Classification of Diseases and Related Health Problems (11th ed. ICD-11; World Health Organization, 2020)
Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press; 2019 Jul 30. p. 678.
The correct answer is: Developmental learning disorder with impairment in reading

questions.question_text: Reactive attachment disorder is generally diagnosed before the age of
questions.explanation:
Reactive attachment disorder (RAD) is characterised by grossly abnormal attachment behaviours in early childhood, occurring in the context of a history of grossly inadequate child care (e.g. severe neglect, maltreatment, institutional deprivation). Even when an adequate primary caregiver is newly available, the child does not turn to the primary caregiver for comfort, support, and nurture; rarely displays security-seeking behaviours towards any adult; and does not respond when comfort is offered. RAD can only be diagnosed in children, and features of the disorder develop within the first 5 years of life. However, the disorder cannot be diagnosed before the age of 1 (or a developmental age of less than 9 months), when the capacity for selective attachments may not be fully developed, or in the context of autism spectrum disorder.
Ref: International Statistical Classification of Diseases and Related Health Problems (11th ed. ICD-11; World Health Organization, 2020)
The correct answer is: 5

questions.question_text: The most common psychiatric co-morbidity associated with Asperger syndrome is
questions.explanation:
Psychiatric comorbidity is high in Asperger syndrome. Depression and anxiety are the most common. Bipolar affective disorder and schizophrenia are more common than in the general population.
Ref: Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press; 2019 Jul 30. p. 820.
The correct answer is: Depression

questions.question_text: Which of the following is considered a protective factor against the development of conduct problems in high-risk children?

options.text: Learning problems before 10 years of age
Having a family member convicted for violent conduct

questions.explanation:
Werner's Kauai Longitudinal Study monitored the impact of a variety of biological and psychosocial risk factors, stressful life events, and protective factors on the development of a multiethnic cohort of 698 children born in 1955 on the 'Garden Island' in the Hawaiian chain. Some 30% of the survivors in the study population were considered high-risk children because they were born in chronic poverty, subjected to perinatal stress, and lived in family environments troubled by chronic discord, divorce, or parental psychopathology. The findings focused on resiliency and its contribution to good developmental outcomes despite high-risk status.
Ref: Werner EE. Resilience in development. Current directions in psychological science. 1995 Jun;4(3):81-4.
The correct answer is: Resilient temperament

questions.question_text: Regarding the aetiology of ADHD, all of the following are true except

options.text: There is a 50% increased risk in monozygotic twins
Siblings of hyperactive children have about twice the increased risk of having the disorder
Predominant serotonin dysregulation is seen in the prefrontal cortex
Neuroimaging shows lower cerebral blood flow and metabolic rates in the frontal lobe areas of children with ADHD than in controls

correct_answer.text: Predominant serotonin dysregulation is seen in the prefrontal cortex

correct_answers.text: Predominant serotonin dysregulation is seen in the prefrontal cortex

questions.explanation:
Many neurotransmitters are likely associated with ADHD symptoms. However, dopamine is a primary focus of clinical investigation, and the prefrontal cortex has been implicated based on its role in attention and regulation of impulse control. Studies have also shown that brain regions such as the locus coeruleus, which consists predominantly of noradrenergic neurons, play a significant role in attention. In part, hypotheses regarding the neurochemistry of ADHD have arisen from the effect of medications. Stimulants, known to be the most effective medications in the treatment of ADHD, affect both dopamine and norepinephrine, leading to neurotransmitter hypotheses that may include dysfunction in both the adrenergic and dopaminergic systems.
Ref: Boland R, Verduin M. Kaplan and Sadock's Synopsis of Psychiatry, 12th Edition. 2022. p. 139.
The correct answer is: Predominant serotonin dysregulation is seen in the prefrontal cortex

questions.question_text: Which of the following suggests a diagnosis of bulimia nervosa rather than anorexia nervosa?
questions.explanation:
There is an increased prevalence of disorders of impulsivity and lack of control in people with bulimia nervosa. Patients who have to satisfy their binges at all costs (e.g. shoplifting) may have issues with impulsivity and rage. People with bulimic illnesses also have a higher prevalence of substance misuse.
Ref: Morris J, Anderson S. An update on eating disorders. BJPsych Advances. 2020:1-11.
The correct answer is: Poor impulse control

questions.question_text: Pica typically occurs during
questions.explanation:
Pica is characterised by the persistent (>1month) eating of non-nutritive substances at a developmentally inappropriate age (>1 year). It typically occurs during the 2nd and 3rd years of life, though may occur in young pregnant women. Common substances include dirt, stones, plastic, paper, hair, faeces, wood, string, etc. Pica is common in people with intellectual disability and autism spectrum disorder. Consequences may include toxicity, infection, or GIT ulceration/obstruction. Hypothesized causes include hunger, malnutrition, nutritional deficiencies, psychosocial stressors, and brain disorders such as lesions in the hypothalamus.
Ref: Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press; 2019 Jul 30. p. 694.
The correct answer is: 2-3 years of age

questions.question_text: A 14-year-old girl presents with some uncoordinated movements of her limbs and emotional lability. She has a history of fever and sore throat six months ago. Which is the most likely cause for her presentation?
questions.explanation:
Sydenham chorea is the major neurological presentation of rheumatic fever, an inflammatory process following infection with group A streptococci (GAS) such as throat infection or scarlet fever. Sydenham chorea is characterised by uncoordinated jerking movements affecting the face and limbs, as well as hypotonia. Some children also experience vocal and motor tics that may persist. Behavioural symptoms and psychiatric co-morbidities are common and can have an abrupt onset that may precede the onset of the chorea. Emotional lability, anxiety, and symptoms of OCD are the most well recognised and there have also been associations with ADHD, mood disorders, and even symptoms of psychosis.
Ref: Warrilow A, Morton M. Autoimmune disorders in child psychiatry: keeping up with the field. BJPsych Advances. 2015 Nov;21(6):367-76.
The correct answer is: Sydenham chorea

questions.question_text: Which of the following treatments is no longer licensed in the UK for children with ADHD?
questions.explanation:
Pemoline is no longer licensed in UK because of the risk of serious hepatotoxicity and death.
Ref: Safer DJ, Zito JM, Gardner JF. Pemoline hepatotoxicity and postmarketing surveillance. Journal of the American Academy of Child & Adolescent Psychiatry. 2001 Jun 1;40(6):622-9.
The correct answer is: Pemoline

questions.question_text: Which drug is now specifically contraindicated in depressed children and adolescents due to an association with increased risk of suicide?
questions.explanation:
Paroxetine and venlafaxine should not be used for the treatment of depression in children and young people, as they have the strongest association with suicide risk.
Ref: National Institute for Health and Clinical Excellence. The NICE guideline on the identification and management of depression in children and young people. 2019.
The correct answer is: Paroxetine

questions.question_text: The most common cause of co-morbidity in children and adolescents with bipolar disorder is
questions.explanation:
Amongst children and adolescents with bipolar disorder, approximately 53% have ADHD, 42% ODD, 23% an anxiety disorder, 27% conduct disorder, and 9% a substance disorder.
Ref: Findling RL et al. Progress in diagnosis and treatment of bipolar disorder among children and adolescents: an international perspective. Evidence-based mental health. 2018 Nov 1;21(4):177-81.
The correct answer is: ADHD

questions.question_text: Manifestations of oppositional defiant disorder are almost invariably present

options.text: In the presence of all adults

questions.explanation:
In oppositional defiant disorder (ODD), a child's temper outbursts, active refusal to comply with rules, and annoying behaviours exceed expectations for these behaviours for children of the same age. The disorder is an enduring pattern of negativistic, hostile, and defiant behaviours in the absence of significant violations of the rights of others. Manifestations of ODD are almost invariably present in the home, but they may not be present at school or with other adults or peers. In some cases, the child has symptoms outside the home from the start. In others, it starts at home and later moves beyond that. Typically, symptoms of the disorder are most evident in interactions with adults or peers whom the child knows well.
Ref: Boland R, Verduin M. Kaplan and Sadock's Synopsis of Psychiatry, 12th Edition. 2022. p. 187.
The correct answer is: At home

questions.question_text: The most common co-morbid disorders seen in Tourette syndrome are
questions.explanation:
90% of patients with Tourette syndrome have at least one co-morbidity. Up to 55% of patients are also diagnosed with ADHD, 50% with OCD, and up to 20% with co-morbid autism spectrum disorder. Males are more likely to have co-morbid disorders than females.
Ref: Robertson MM. Tourette syndrome in children and adolescents: aetiology, presentation and treatment. BJPsych Advances. 2016 May;22(3):165-75.
Yang Z et al. Investigating shared genetic basis across tourette syndrome and comorbid neurodevelopmental disorders along the impulsivity-compulsivity spectrum. Biological psychiatry. 2021 Sep 1;90(5):317-27.
The correct answer is: ADHD and OCD

questions.question_text: The most common co-morbidity in children with Tourette syndrome is
questions.explanation:
90% of patients with Tourette syndrome have at least one co-morbidity. Up to 55% of patients are also diagnosed with ADHD, 50% with OCD, and up to 20% with co-morbid autism spectrum disorder. Males are more likely to have co-morbid disorders than females. ADHD symptoms may appear 2–3 years before the onset of tics. The patten of comorbidity may differ between adults and children. While in children, ADHD, ASD, OCD, and oppositional defiant disorder (ODD) are more common, in adults the predominant comorbidities are OCD and mood disorders.
Ref: Robertson MM. Tourette syndrome in children and adolescents: aetiology, presentation and treatment. BJPsych Advances. 2016 May;22(3):165-75.
Szejko N, Müller-Vahl KR. Challenges in the diagnosis and assessment in patients with Tourette syndrome and comorbid obsessive-compulsive disorder. Neuropsychiatric Disease and Treatment. 2021 Apr 30:1253-66.
The correct answer is: ADHD

questions.question_text: Which of the following has been found to be effective in treating adolescent inhalant abuse?
questions.explanation:
Adolescent inhalant abuse is characterised by the use of gases, glues, and/or aerosols to achieve intoxication. Inhalants are frequently one of the first drugs to be used by adolescents due to ease of access, lack of penalties association with possession, and rapid onset of effects. First-line treatment for adolescent inhalant abuse is multimodal, including individual CBT, family therapy, and activity and engagement programs.
Ref: Nguyen J, O'Brien C, Schapp S. Adolescent inhalant use prevention, assessment, and treatment: A literature synthesis. International Journal of Drug Policy. 2016 May 1;31:15-24.
The correct answer is: No known pharmacotherapy

questions.question_text: Which of the following should be used as a first choice treatment in adolescents with acute manic or mixed episodes?
questions.explanation:
Aripiprazole and lithium are the only licensed medications for treating mania. In practice, lithium is not generally used acutely in the treatment of manic/mixed episodes in adolescents, as it requires commitment to longer-term treatment and regular blood tests. NICE guidelines (updated 2020) recommend considering aripiprazole or using an alternative antipsychotic (e.g. risperidone, olanzapine, quetiapine) in accordance with guidance for adults and limiting drug treatment to 12 weeks. It is unclear whether valproate has the same beneficial effects on mania in young people as it does in adults. NICE recommends that valproate monotherapy should NOT be used for first-line management of mania and it should NOT be offered to girls or young women of childbearing potential because of teratogenic effects and the risk of polycystic ovary syndrome.
Ref: National Institute for Health and Clinical Excellence. The NICE guideline on the assessment and management of bipolar disorder in adults, children and young people in primary and secondary care. Updated edition 2020.
Findling RL et al. Progress in diagnosis and treatment of bipolar disorder among children and adolescents: an international perspective. Evidence-based mental health. 2018 Nov 1;21(4):177-81.
The correct answer is: Olanzapine

questions.question_text: Which neurotransmitter system is commonly postulated to be involved in the aetiology of Tourette syndrome?
questions.explanation:
The aetiology of Tourette syndrome includes genetic factors and environmental influences (infections and neuroimmunological effects, pre- and/or perinatal difficulties, psychosocial stressors, and androgen influences). No single gene has been identified (likely more than one gene). An association with psychosocial stress is well known. Heightened HPA axis and noradrenergic system reactivity have been demonstrated. There is a likely disturbance of the dopamine system. Other aetiological possibilities include gestational and perinatal insults, exposure to androgens, heat, fatigue, and post-infectious autoimmune mechanisms.
Ref: Robertson MM. Tourette syndrome in children and adolescents: aetiology, presentation and treatment. BJPsych Advances. 2016 May;22(3):165-75.
Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press; 2019 Jul 30. p. 676.
The correct answer is: Dopamine

questions.question_text: Which of the following is the evidence-based, first-line treatment for OCD in children?
questions.explanation:
Children with OCD and mild functional impairment should initially be offered self-help guides. If self-help does not work, or for those with mild-moderate impairment, CBT with exposure and response prevention (ERP) should be offered first-line. CBT interventions include learning about the nature of intrusive thoughts, exposure to worrying or disturbing thoughts (obsessions), and finding out how the cycles of behaviour and emotions cause the repetitive behaviours (compulsions) to persist. If CBT is inadequate, or for those with severe impairment, medication should be added. Combination therapy (CBT plus SSRI) has not been shown to be more effective than CBT alone, regardless of initial symptom severity. However, combination therapy is more effective than an SSRI alone.
Ref: Öst LG, Riise EN, Wergeland GJ, Hansen B, Kvale G. Cognitive behavioral and pharmacological treatments of OCD in children: A systematic review and meta-analysis. Journal of Anxiety Disorders. 2016 Oct 1;43:58-69.
National Institute for Health and Clinical Excellence. The NICE guideline on core interventions in the treatment of obsessive-compulsive disorder and body dysmorphic disorder. Updated 2020.
Williams TI, Shafran R. Obsessive–compulsive disorder in young people. BJPsych Advances. 2015 May;21(3):196-205.
The correct answer is: CBT

questions.question_text: The total sleeping time of a newborn baby is approximately
questions.explanation:
Most newborns (0-3 months) sleep 14-17 hours per day.
Ref: Bathory E, Tomopoulos S. Sleep regulation, physiology and development, sleep duration and patterns, and sleep hygiene in infants, toddlers, and preschool-age children. Current problems in pediatric and adolescent health care. 2017 Feb 1;47(2):29-42.
The correct answer is: 14-17 hours per day

questions.question_text: Which is the first line drug in an 8-year-old with uncomplicated ADHD?
questions.explanation:
Methylphenidate (stimulant) is recommended as first-line medication (either short- or long-acting preparation) in children and young people with ADHD by NICE guidelines (updated 2018).
Ref: National Institute for Health and Clinical Excellence. The NICE guideline on the diagnosis and management of attention deficit hyperactivity disorder. 2018.
The correct answer is: Methylphenidate

questions.question_text: Which of the following may be a long-term effect of prescribing high doses of methylphenidate over long periods without drug holidays?
questions.explanation:
Stimulant medication, including methylphenidate, commonly suppresses appetite during the day. This is occasionally associated with slowing of weight growth and, less commonly, with slowing of height growth. NICE recommends that if a child or young person's height over time is significantly affected by medication (i.e. they have not met height expected for age), a planned break in treatment over school holidays should be considered.
Ref: National Institute for Health and Clinical Excellence. The NICE guideline on the diagnosis and management of attention deficit hyperactivity disorder. 2018.
Hill P. Attention-deficit hyperactivity disorder in children and adolescents: Assessment and treatment. BJPsych Advances. 2015 Jan;21(1):23-30.
The correct answer is: Growth slowing

questions.question_text: The commonest age of presentation for school refusal is
questions.explanation:
School refusal is characterised by refusal to go to school or stay in school, even when under pressure from parents and school authorities. It is not a psychiatric disorder per se and can have many causes; it is considered a problem rather than a diagnosis. School refusal may occur in a young child who is first entering school or in an older child or adolescent who is making a transition into a new grade or school. The peak age is 11-13 years. The incidence in children and adolescents reported to be 1-5%, with the sex distribution equal.
Ref: Boland R, Verduin M. Kaplan and Sadock's Synopsis of Psychiatry, 12th Edition. 2022. p. 896.
Elliott JG, Place M. Practitioner review: school refusal: developments in conceptualisation and treatment since 2000. Journal of Child Psychology and Psychiatry. 2019 Jan;60(1):4-15.
The correct answer is: 11 years

questions.question_text: Which of the following disorders is more common in females?

options.text: Developmental language disorder with impairment of receptive and expressive language
Developmental learning disorder with impairment in written expression
Developmental learning disorder with impairment in mathematics
Developmental learning disorder with impairment in reading
Developmental language disorder with impairment of mainly expressive language

correct_answer.text: Developmental learning disorder with impairment in mathematics

correct_answers.text: Developmental learning disorder with impairment in mathematics

questions.explanation:
Developmental learning disorder with impairment in mathematics is characterised by significant and persistent difficulties in learning academic skills related to mathematics or arithmetic, such as number sense, memorisation of number facts, accurate calculation, fluent calculation, and accurate mathematic reasoning. The individual's performance in mathematics or arithmetic is markedly below what would be expected for chronological or developmental age and level of intellectual functioning and results in significant impairment in functioning. 1-6% of school-age children are affected, with female predominance. It is often associated with visuospatial deficits and attributed to right parietal dysfunction.
Ref: International Statistical Classification of Diseases and Related Health Problems (11th ed. ICD-11; World Health Organization, 2020)
Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press; 2019 Jul 30. p. 678.
The correct answer is: Developmental learning disorder with impairment in mathematics

questions.question_text: All of the following are risk factors for adolescent suicide except
questions.explanation:
Rates of suicide in the UK have increased among adolescents by approximately 7.9% each year between 2010 and 2017. Rates among females have increased at a higher rate, though absolute number of deaths is still lower among young women than young men. Completed suicide is more common in males, while suicide attempts and self-harm are more common in females. Other risk factors for adolescent suicide include depression, struggles with sexuality or gender, aggression and impulsivity, difficulties in peer relationships, family difficulties, sleep difficulties, history of self-harm and/or attempted suicide, parental psychopathology & suicidal behaviour, and substance misuse (including alcohol).
Ref: Correia R, Jackson D. Risk to self: identifying and managing risk of suicide and self-harm. BJPsych Advances. 2020:1-11.
Bould H et al. Rising suicide rates among adolescents in England and Wales. The Lancet. 2019 Jul 13;394(10193):116-7.
Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press; 2019 Jul 30. pp. 698-699.
The correct answer is: Female sex

questions.question_text: Which of the following is associated with conduct disorder?
questions.explanation:
Studies of conduct-disordered juvenile offenders have found high plasma serotonin levels in the blood. Evidence indicates that blood serotonin levels correlate inversely with levels of 5-HIAA in the CSF and that low 5-HIAA levels in the CSF correlate with aggression and violence.
Ref: Boland R, Verduin M. Kaplan and Sadock's Synopsis of Psychiatry, 12th Edition. 2022. p. 194.
The correct answer is: Low CSF serotonin

questions.question_text: Which of the following symptoms of mania is least commonly reported in children with bipolar disorder?
questions.explanation:
Symptoms of mania commonly reported in children with bipolar disorder include increased energy, irritability, mood lability, distractibility, goal-directed activity, euphoria/elated mood, pressured speech, hyperactivity, racing thoughts, poor judgement, grandiosity, inappropriate laughter decreased need for sleep, and flight of ideas.
Ref: Findling RL et al. Progress in diagnosis and treatment of bipolar disorder among children and adolescents: an international perspective. Evidence-based mental health. 2018 Nov 1;21(4):177-81.
The correct answer is: Hypersexuality

questions.question_text: Developmentally inappropriate social relatedness seen before the age of 5 following prolonged separation from caregivers is seen in
questions.explanation:
Disinhibited social engagement disorder is newly described in both DSM-5 and ICD-11. It is characterised by a pattern of behaviour in which a child actively approaches and interacts with unfamiliar adults in an overly familiar way. These children may display reduced/absent reticence in approaching/interacting with unfamiliar adults; overly familiar verbal of physical behaviour; diminished/absent checking back with an adult caregiver; and willingness to go off with unfamiliar adults with little to no hesitation. These children have experienced patterns of extremes of insufficient care (e.g. social neglect or deprivation, repeated changes of primary caregivers, rearing in institutions or other settings that severely limit opportunities to form selective attachment).
Ref: International Statistical Classification of Diseases and Related Health Problems (11th ed. ICD-11; World Health Organization, 2020)
The correct answer is: Disinhibited social engagement disorder

questions.question_text: The prevalence of ADHD among girls in the UK between the ages of 5-15 is
questions.explanation:
The UK prevalence for ADHD is just under 5%; 3-4% in boys and just under 1% in girls (four times more common in boys).
Ref: Hill P. Attention-deficit hyperactivity disorder in children and adolescents: Assessment and treatment. BJPsych Advances. 2015 Jan;21(1):23-30.
The correct answer is: 0-1%

questions.question_text: The overall prevalence of psychiatric disorders in adolescence is
questions.explanation:
Adolescence, defined as a transitional phase between ages 10 and 19, is sometimes perceived as a phase of life with no health problems. However, approximately 20% of adolescents experience a mental health problem, most commonly depression or anxiety.
Ref: Silva SA et al. Common mental disorders prevalence in adolescents: A systematic review and meta-analyses. PloS one. 2020 Apr 23;15(4):e0232007.
The correct answer is: 16-20%

questions.question_text: From a developmental perspective, suicidal ideation is rare before the age of
questions.explanation:
From a developmental perspective, suicidal ideation is rare before 10 years of age, increases slowly through age 12 years, and then accelerates through age 17 years.
Ref: Benton TD et al. Dysregulation and suicide in children and adolescents. Child and Adolescent Psychiatric Clinics. 2021 Apr 1;30(2):389-99.
The correct answer is: 10 years

questions.question_text: Approximately what percentage of school-aged children are affected by developmental dyslexia?
questions.explanation:
Developmental learning disorder with impairment in reading (developmental dyslexia) is characterised by significant and persistent difficulties in learning academic skills related to reading, such as word reading accuracy, reading fluency, and reading comprehension. The individual's performance in reading is markedly below what would be expected for chronological age and level of intellectual functioning and results in significant impairment in functioning. 4% of school-age children are affected. There is male predominance [4:1] and often a family history. Approximately 20% of children have co-morbid CD or ADHD.
Ref: International Statistical Classification of Diseases and Related Health Problems (11th ed. ICD-11; World Health Organization, 2020)
Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press; 2019 Jul 30. p. 678.
The correct answer is: 4%

questions.question_text: Tom is a 7-year-old boy who was recently diagnosed with ADHD. His mum wants to know about the long term prognosis. Which of the following symptoms is most likely to remit first?
questions.explanation:
A proportion of children with ADHD will improve with maturation. Although hyperactivity wanes with age, impulsivity and inattention do so at a slower rate. About 15% of children who show a full ADHD picture in late childhood will have a full diagnosis in early adult life. 50% will show an attenuated picture characterized by troublesome inattentiveness, impulsiveness, and personal disorganisation.
Ref: Hill P. Attention-deficit hyperactivity disorder in children and adolescents: Assessment and treatment. BJPsych Advances. 2015 Jan;21(1):23-30.
The correct answer is: Hyperactivity

questions.question_text: Along with emotional disorders, the most common psychiatric disorder(s) seen in childhood in the Isle of Wight studies was/were
questions.explanation:
The Isle of Wight studies began in 1964-65 with a series of epidemiological studies of educational, psychiatric, and physical disorders in children. About 7% of 10- to 12-year-old children showed a psychiatric disorder of sufficient severity. Emotional disorders and disturbances of conduct were the commonest conditions and occurred with the same frequency. Emotional disorders were slightly more common in girls, while conduct disorders were much more common in boys.
Ref: Rutter M, Tizard J, Yule W, Graham P, Whitmore K. Isle of Wight studies, 1964–1974. Psychological medicine. 1976 May;6(2):313-32.
The correct answer is: Conduct disorders

questions.question_text: The Cambridge study by Farrington et al. identified risk factors in children between 8-10 years that can predict later delinquent behaviour by the age of 32. Which one among the following is not a risk factor identified by this study?
questions.explanation:
The most important predictors, at age 8-10, of later delinquency from the Cambridge study:
-       Antisocial child behaviour, including troublesomeness in school, dishonesty, and aggressiveness
-       Hyperactivity-impulsivity-attention deficit
-       Low intelligence and poor school attainment
-       Family criminality
-       Family poverty
-       Poor parental child-rearing behaviour
Ref: Farrington DP. The Twelfth Jack Tizard Memorial Lecture* The development of offending and antisocial behaviour from childhood: Key findings from the Cambridge study in delinquent development. Journal of Child Psychology and Psychiatry. 1995 Sep;36(6):929-64.
The correct answer is: Parental depression
